en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Admonition to the King, translated by Juqu Jingsheng, Marquis of Anyang of the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a king named Asita-Seni who, while traveling through his realm, passed by the place where the Buddha was staying; with his body covered in dust, he unsheathed his sword, set aside his parasol, and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Celestial Honored One said,
"Be seated. The King then sat down.
The Buddha asked the king, "From where have you come, O King? Your body is covered in dust.
The king then withdrew to sit, prostrated himself, and replied:
“Very well! Should any calamities or anomalies occur within the borders of your kingdom, [inform me].
The Buddha said to the king:

"A king should govern by means of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and must not lose his sense of propriety; he should always nurture the people with a heart of compassion, for it is by this that one attains hegemonic rule.
That those who become kings do so is entirely due to the performance of good deeds in past lives; in administering civil affairs, one must not be partial or unjust."

From the high ministers and various officials down to the common people, all have words of resentment; the King’s governance is unjust, and the whole world is filled with indignation. When his life ends, his spirit will inevitably enter the Tai Shan hell, and though he may repent later, it will be too late to avail him.

When a king governs his country with impartiality and constant moderation, his subjects and citizens praise his virtue and the four seas turn their hearts toward him; even the devas, nāgas, and spirits hear of the king’s goodness, and having died to ascend to heaven, he has no regrets thereafter.

A king should not indulge in lewdness to bring about his own ruin, nor should he harbor resentment to commit acts of cruelty; he ought to accept the loyal and upright admonitions of his ministers. Furthermore, when speaking with others, he should always be broad-minded and composed, never acting with passion or heat.
"One should attend to the people with four intentions. What are these four?

To provide them with grain at the appropriate times; to speak to them with a harmonious mind; to share all precious treasures with the people; and to look after the elderly, the sick, and the widowed."

If a king acts in this manner, peace will prevail within his kingdom and he shall obtain its blessings; at the end of his life, he will ascend to heaven, and his aspirations will be spontaneously fulfilled.

Yet, a king cannot maintain such sovereignty forever; though all people revere him and find joy in him, even his famous elephants, fine horses, precious chariots, and worthy ministers—along with the assembly of officials and attendants leading and following before and behind, as well as the inner treasury of rare jewels, granaries, and all manner of goods—all these must eventually decay and perish, for nothing endures forever.

"The young shall grow old; the strong must fall ill; all living beings are destined to return to death. Precious treasures, wives, children, and those within and without the household cannot be possessed forever. It is like a person who dreams of palaces, beautiful gardens, trees, flowers, fruits, ponds, and flowing springs, playing therein with boundless joy; yet upon waking, it vanishes suddenly and one knows not where it is. All that exists in this world is like such a dream."
"O King, have you not seen that though trees bear flowers and fruit, those flowers and fruits cannot remain forever upon them; the lush green leaves will inevitably wither and fall;
celestial crowns, turbans, and finely embroidered robes cannot remain forever beautiful; flowing water cannot remain forever full;
and when fire is set in the wilderness, its fierce and blazing flames do not last long before they are extinguished?"

Violent winds, torrential rains, and thunderbolts may vanish in an instant; when the sun is about to rise, the stars lose their brilliance, and the sun’s intense radiance, though it illuminates the world, soon turns to darkness. The impermanence of the world is likewise thus.

It is like a great stone mountain on each of the four sides, with six mountains from above and below all arriving at once and converging together; within it, all sentient beings, whether noble or lowly, will be ground to powder and crushed.
“There are four things for which a person cannot find a cessation:

when old age arrives, the body withers; when illness comes, the mind is afflicted; when the body dies, the spirit departs; and all precious treasures must eventually be abandoned and cannot be preserved. These four arrive one after another and cannot be avoided or escaped; they cannot be averted by verbal pleas or apologies, nor can they be resolved through wealth or entreaties.”

At that time, with all the famous elephants, fine horses, rare treasures, valiant warriors, and the assembly of ministers and officials escorting him from front and back, who would be able to repel or obstruct the king?

"Your Majesty, have you not seen the lion, the most ferocious among beasts? When it sees a herd of deer from afar that it wishes to seize, it advances, pounces, tears them apart, and devours their flesh; how can such agony even be described?"

Life is like a lion seizing a herd of deer; when a person’s life is about to end, the body becomes restless, the blood vessels wither, and the complexion changes. As the days of life draw near their close, the five viscera lose their harmony and one loses all appetite for food and drink. At such a time, even divine mantras, skilled physicians, and excellent medicines cannot bring about a cure.

Their mouths utter false speech, yet whatever they demand, their families indulge them. Their bodies ache all over as if they have been flogged and tortured; their hands and feet are twisted and contorted, and their joints feel as if they would come apart. Their mouths are parched, their breathing is labored, and they are so emaciated and debilitated that they cannot rise or sit, nor lie down or sleep without another’s assistance.

Even if they obtain excellent medicine, gruel, or sweet food, which others must hold for them, they inevitably suffer extreme agony again, as if their sinews and veins were about to snap. There is only the breath going out, with no more returning in; their lips are dry and withered, their vital energy is utterly exhausted, and only the pathogenic qi remains.

The tongue retracts slightly, the face loses its color, and the ears and nose become blocked so that one no longer hears sounds or smells scents. The hands and feet are cramped and the tendons are taut; the mouth is clenched so that one wishes to speak but cannot. The hands may grasp at empty space, unable to search for anything nearby. Profuse cold sweat flows from the body and tears stream continuously from the eyes. The mind is gripped by pain and consciousness fades away until nothing more is known; the warmth departs, the body grows cold, and the soul has left.

All precious treasures, parents, brothers, wives, internal and external acquaintances, and servants must all be abandoned; one departs alone following [the path], not knowing where one will arrive, for though the world is pleasant, one cannot remain there long.
"At this time, what should the King rely upon? He should rely solely on filial piety and compassionate care for his two parents;

he should serve śramaṇas of noble conduct and pure virtue; when seeing ordinary elders, he should respect them; he should share all his wealth and treasures with the people in joy; he should bestow kindness upon the people with a compassionate heart; he must not use slanderous words to harm the lives of the people; as the law of a king, he should proclaim the Holy Way and teach the people to do good; he should maintain a single mind, keeping his thoughts fixed upon the Triple Gem."
When a king is thus, all the sages offer their praise; devas, nāgas, and spirits protect his kingdom; he enjoys honor and renown during life and attains rebirth in heaven after death.
"When the body dies and the spirit departs, what can one rely upon? One can rely only on the wholesome. When a fire blazes fiercely, one relies on water to extinguish it;

a person suffering from hunger and thirst relies only on water and grain; the aged rely on a stool and a staff; the blind rely on those with sight; those in darkness rely on lamps and fire; those afflicted by severe illness rely on a skilled physician and medicine; a ship sailing upon the great ocean when wind and waves are violent relies on its rudders and oars; and when there are bandits on the road, one relies on a place of concealment."

When the body dies and the spirit departs, one relies solely upon the cultivation of goodness; just as when encountering those hardships, each relied upon their own affairs to extricate themselves and achieve salvation, so that the royal house obtained peace.

The King found no lasting joy in food and drink of the most exquisite flavors, nor in the freedom of his travels and dwellings, which cannot be maintained forever; nor in the satiety that must all eventually dissipate, which cannot be maintained forever;

nor in the fragrant perfumes smeared on his body that fill the nostrils, the pearls and necklaces that dazzle the eyes, or the beautiful flowers from land and water used for adornment, or the famous garments woven with golden thread—whether they be white woolen robes, embroidered brocades, variegated silks, "infinite" robes, fine cottons, delicate fabrics, or patterned damasks—all these are impermanent and cannot be preserved for long.

"Palaces, observatories, lofty terraces, magnificent gates, and halls; couches and seats made of gold, silver, and the seven treasures; woolen rugs, carpets, and fine, soft silken spreads upon which the body rests; curtains and canopies woven from the seven treasures with embroidered patterns and brocades; pillars, beams, and palace doors carved and engraved with intricate designs; and the burning of various blended incenses while sporting therein—all these are impermanent and cannot be maintained for long."

"The gathering of various sounds from lutes, zithers, harps, and flutes, and the profusion of voices from singing, dancing, and performers filling the ears with joy beyond description—even these are impermanent; they are like illusions and like dreams, unable to be maintained for long."

Regarding the sight of the precious elephant, horse, and chariot with radiant eyes: when the King goes forth, bells are struck and drums are beaten as he is escorted by couriers before and behind. The King rides in a carriage with a feathered canopy, while attendants hold banners; their handles are adorned with emerald feathers and peacock plumes to sweep away dust. The roads are leveled and filled, and the railings are painted vermilion. Among the masses who behold this, there are none who do not feel awe and reverence; they welcome the King with beautiful flowers and famous incenses, chanting "Long live the Emperor for ten thousand years"—yet even this is difficult to preserve forever.
"Does Your Majesty not see when a person is about to die?

People from within and without their families gather around them, beating their breasts and crying out to Heaven, all saying, 'Alas! What can be done? They sob and choke with emotion as tears flow down their cheeks, wailing, 'How painful it is!
Our spirit has departed alone: how will you leave us like this!'"
"Those who hear of this are without exception moved to grief; those who see it are without exception moved to join in their lamentation.

It has been carried out of the city and cast into the wilderness, where flying birds and running beasts claw and tear at it for food. Worms within the body devour its flesh; scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, the bones have all become dry. Formerly, the various kings were honored, illustrious, and noble—their processions were deep and resonant, just like those of Your Majesty—yet today they have vanished utterly, leaving nothing to be seen."
These are all clear proofs of impermanence. It has always been thus in antiquity, how much more so today;

Your Majesty should reflect upon this deeply. Do not harbor lustful thoughts, nor accept the words of flatterers that lead innocent people into guilt. You should accept loyal admonitions and govern with moderation. You should fear the agonizing torments of the hells and refrain from killing any living creature, for all beings that possess blood cherish their lives.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, the king’s mind was immediately liberated, and he wished to become a disciple.
He then received the five precepts and, bowing his head to the ground, paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Admonition to the King Spoken by the Buddha
